claim: GAD67-GFP knock-in mice were crossed with Thy1-jRGECO1a mice to produce a GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse.
source: GAD67-GFP knock-in mice on a Swiss Webster background were crossed with Thy1-jRGECO1a mice to produce a GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse, which was used to visualize GABAergic modules, to identify the dense network of GABAergic neurons and terminals in modules of the LC in the green channel (Tamamaki et al., 2003) and the calcium indicator, jRGECO1a, in the red channel (Dana et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the mouse breeding strategy used to generate the experimental animals.

claim: The GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse was used to visualize GABAergic modules in the LC in the green channel.
source: GAD67-GFP knock-in mice on a Swiss Webster background were crossed with Thy1-jRGECO1a mice to produce a GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse, which was used to visualize GABAergic modules, to identify the dense network of GABAergic neurons and terminals in modules of the LC in the green channel (Tamamaki et al., 2003) and the calcium indicator, jRGECO1a, in the red channel (Dana et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of GFP expression to identify GABAergic modules, supported by citation to Tamamaki et al., 2003.

claim: The calcium indicator jRGECO1a was visualized in the red channel in the GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse.
source: GAD67-GFP knock-in mice on a Swiss Webster background were crossed with Thy1-jRGECO1a mice to produce a GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse, which was used to visualize GABAergic modules, to identify the dense network of GABAergic neurons and terminals in modules of the LC in the green channel (Tamamaki et al., 2003) and the calcium indicator, jRGECO1a, in the red channel (Dana et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of jRGECO1a as a calcium indicator, supported by citation to Dana et al., 2018.

claim: A standard craniotomy was performed with modifications to suit the specific characteristics of the IC.
source: A standard craniotomy was performed (Goldey et al., 2014) with modifications to suit the specific characteristics of the IC in terms of its location, depth, and high density of the surrounding vasculature (Xiong et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the surgical procedure with citations to previous methods.

claim: The IC sits deeper in the brain compared to the surrounding structures.
source: Because the IC sits deeper in the brain compared to the surrounding structures, the direct insertion of the 45° microprism was found to push the IC ventrally.
evidence: The manuscript describes an anatomical observation that influenced the surgical approach.

claim: Direct insertion of the 45° microprism was found to push the IC ventrally.
source: Because the IC sits deeper in the brain compared to the surrounding structures, the direct insertion of the 45° microprism was found to push the IC ventrally.
evidence: The manuscript reports an experimental observation from the surgical procedure.

claim: A fine diamond knife was used to separate the lateral surface of the IC from the surrounding tissues without damaging the transverse and sigmoid sinuses.
source: Therefore, a fine diamond knife was used to separate the lateral surface of the IC from the surrounding tissues without damaging the transverse and sigmoid sinuses (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript describes a surgical technique with reference to figure panels showing the procedure.

claim: Filling the gap between the skull surface and the microprism with saline was found to generate motion artifact due to heart pulsation.
source: Filling the gap between the skull surface and the microprism with saline was found to generate motion artifact due to the heart pulsation, so 1% agarose was used to fill the gap to reduce the motion artifact and add more stability to the microprism (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript reports an experimental observation that led to a methodological modification.

claim: 1% agarose was used to fill the gap between the skull surface and the microprism to reduce motion artifact and add stability.
source: Filling the gap between the skull surface and the microprism with saline was found to generate motion artifact due to the heart pulsation, so 1% agarose was used to fill the gap to reduce the motion artifact and add more stability to the microprism (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript describes a methodological solution to an experimental problem.

claim: Direct imaging of the dorsal surface of the IC was conducted by scanning the DC surface from the most medial to lateral regions following the convex curvature of the surface.
source: To compare response properties between the LC and DC, direct imaging (i.e. without a microprism) of the dorsal surface of the IC, where the DC is located, was also conducted by scanning the DC surface from the most medial to lateral regions following the convex curvature of the surface (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: The manuscript describes the imaging approach for the DC with reference to figure panels.

claim: The 920 nm laser beam was initially used to scan for GFP expressed in GABAergic cells of GAD67-GFP knock-in mice.
source: Therefore, the 920 nm laser beam was initially used to scan for GFP, which is expressed in the GABAergic cells of GAD67-GFP knock-in mice.
evidence: The manuscript describes the imaging parameters used to visualize GFP.

claim: The 2P images of the GFP signals from the LC imaged via the microprism revealed the LC characteristic GABAergic modules.
source: The 2P images of the GFP signals from the LC imaged via the microprism, or for simplicity LC(microprism), across different animals revealed the LC characteristic GABAergic modules (Figure 2C and E, the irregular white lines), which were consistent with previous 3D reconstructions of modules from the coronal sections (Chernock et al., 2004; Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging results that are consistent with previous anatomical studies, supported by citations.

claim: The GABAergic modules revealed by 2P imaging were consistent with previous 3D reconstructions of modules from coronal sections.
source: The 2P images of the GFP signals from the LC imaged via the microprism, or for simplicity LC(microprism), across different animals revealed the LC characteristic GABAergic modules (Figure 2C and E, the irregular white lines), which were consistent with previous 3D reconstructions of modules from the coronal sections (Chernock et al., 2004; Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript compares current imaging results with previous anatomical studies, supported by citations.

claim: A laser lesion was created via the microprism to validate the microprism location.
source: To further validate the microprism location and the ability to image the LC from the lateral surface, a laser lesion (see Materials and methods) was created via the microprism (Figure 2G), which was validated histologically (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript describes a validation method with reference to figure panels showing the lesion.

claim: The laser lesion created via the microprism was validated histologically.
source: To further validate the microprism location and the ability to image the LC from the lateral surface, a laser lesion (see Materials and methods) was created via the microprism (Figure 2G), which was validated histologically (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript describes histological validation of the laser lesion with reference to a figure panel.

claim: Most of the dorsal surface of the IC showed a non-clustered distribution of GABAergic cells.
source: For comparison, the whole dorsal surface of the IC was scanned from medial to lateral borders (Figure 2B, the dotted white lines). Unlike the LC, most of the dorsal surface of the IC showed a non-clustered distribution of the GABAergic cells (Figure 2D and F, blue boxes).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations comparing the LC and DC with reference to figure panels.

claim: The lateral horizon of the IC dorsal surface showed clusters of GABAergic cells and terminals that were confirmed to be modules.
source: However, the lateral horizon of the IC dorsal surface showed clusters of GABAergic cells and terminals that were confirmed to be modules, which comprise the prominent feature of the LC (Figure 2D and F, red boxes).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with reference to figure panels.

claim: A laser lesion was created in a GABAergic module located in the dorsolateral surface of the IC and confirmed histologically.
source: To further validate the presence of GABAergic modules in the dorsolateral surface of the IC, a laser lesion was created in a GABAergic module located in that area (Figure 2I and J, dotted red circle), which was confirmed histologically (Figure 2K), demonstrating that it is possible to image a portion of the LC directly from its dorsal surface.
evidence: The manuscript describes a validation experiment with histological confirmation, with reference to figure panels.

claim: It is possible to image a portion of the LC directly from its dorsal surface.
source: To further validate the presence of GABAergic modules in the dorsolateral surface of the IC, a laser lesion was created in a GABAergic module located in that area (Figure 2I and J, dotted red circle), which was confirmed histologically (Figure 2K), demonstrating that it is possible to image a portion of the LC directly from its dorsal surface.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the laser lesion validation experiment.

claim: The GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse showed a non-clustered cellular expression of jRGECO1a on the surface of the DC.
source: Using the 1040 nm laser, the GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse showed a non-clustered cellular expression of jRGECO1a on the surface of the DC (Figure 3A) or on the surface of the LC(microprism) (Figure 3B), as expected.
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with reference to figure panels.

claim: The GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse showed a non-clustered cellular expression of jRGECO1a on the surface of the LC(microprism).
source: Using the 1040 nm laser, the GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mouse showed a non-clustered cellular expression of jRGECO1a on the surface of the DC (Figure 3A) or on the surface of the LC(microprism) (Figure 3B), as expected.
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with reference to figure panels.

claim: Acoustic stimulation paradigms successfully elicited transient cellular calcium signals that varied depending on the stimulus type.
source: As shown by two representative cells from the DC imaged from the dorsal surface or LC imaged via microprism, these acoustic stimulation paradigms successfully elicited transient cellular calcium signals that varied depending on the stimulus type (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results showing calcium responses to acoustic stimuli with reference to figure panels.

claim: The DC and LC have a similar fraction of cells expressing jRGECO1a.
source: The DC and LC have a similar fraction of cells expressing jRGECO1a (paired sample t-test, t(9) = 0.98, p=0.34, n=10 coronal sections from 2 animals) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical comparison of jRGECO1a expression between DC and LC with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The cells expressing jRGECO1a in all regions of the IC were only non-GABAergic neurons.
source: Also, the cells expressing jRGECO1a in all regions of the IC were only non-GABAergic neurons as they did not express GFP which is expressed exclusively in the GABAergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observation about the cell types expressing jRGECO1a with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Imaging the LC via microprism showed clusters of GABAergic modules that take different irregular shapes on the surface of the LC.
source: As indicated by the GFP signals and consistent with Figure 2, imaging the LC of the hybrid mice via microprism showed clusters of GABAergic modules, which take different irregular shapes on the surface of the LC (Figure 4A – irregular white lines).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations with reference to a figure panel.

claim: An inconsistent and fragmentary tonotopic organization was seen over the LC(microprism) based on the best pure tone frequency of each responsive cell.
source: Based on the best pure tone frequency (BTF) of each responsive cell (Barnstedt et al., 2015), an inconsistent and fragmentary tonotopic organization was seen over the LC(microprism) (Figure 4B) as indicated by a low R2 of the best linear and quadratic regressions fit made between the BTFs of cells and their locations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of tonotopic organization with reference to figure panels and a citation to a previous method.

claim: The best fit of the regressions for tonotopic organization in the LC was found to be along different axes across the tested animals.
source: Additionally, the best fit of these regressions was found to be along different axes across the tested animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis results with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Cells in the modules were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than those in the matrix.
source: Despite this inconsistent topographical organization, it was found that the cells in the modules were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than those in the matrix (Mann-Whitney test: z=4.03, p=5.6 × 10–5, a median of best-tuned frequency = 10 and 7.1 Hz for modules [215 cells from 7 animals] and matrix [230 cells from 7 animals], respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical comparison of frequency tuning between modules and matrix.

claim: The DC showed a tonotopic organization of cells along the rostromedial to caudolateral axis tuned to lower or higher frequencies, respectively.
source: Based on the BTF of each responsive cell (Barnstedt et al., 2015), the DC showed a tonotopic organization of cells along the rostromedial to caudolateral axis tuned to lower or higher frequencies, respectively (Figure 4D), as indicated by a high R2 of the regression fits made between BTFs of cells and their locations along the rostromedial to caudolateral axis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of tonotopic organization in the DC with reference to figure panels and a citation.

claim: The R2 of the nonlinear quadratic regression for DC tonotopy was higher than that of the linear fit.
source: It was noted that the R2 of the nonlinear quadratic regression was higher than that of the linear fit.
evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of regression models for tonotopic organization.

claim: A large area of the DC was tuned to the lowest tested frequency (5 kHz), suggesting a low-frequency bias on the surface of the DC.
source: It was also noticed that a large area of the DC was tuned to the lowest tested frequency (5 kHz), suggesting a low-frequency bias on the surface of the DC.
evidence: The manuscript reports an observation and draws an inference about frequency bias in the DC.

claim: The DC showed a low-frequency bias similar to previous work.
source: To quantify tuning differences between DC and LC, the cumulative distribution function based on the cells' BTFs showed a low-frequency bias in the DC, similar to previous work (Ito et al., 2014; Romand and Ehret, 1990; Shen et al., 2003; Stiebler and Ehret, 1985).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis results that are consistent with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Around 50% of the cells of LC(microprism) showed a low-frequency bias to 5 and 7.1 kHz.
source: Although around 50% of the cells of LC(microprism) showed a low-frequency bias to 5 and 7.1 kHz, collectively, most of the LC cells were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than those of the DC (Figure 5A, Mann-Whitney test: z=–11.34, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis results with statistical comparison and reference to a figure panel.

claim: Most of the LC cells were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than those of the DC.
source: Although around 50% of the cells of LC(microprism) showed a low-frequency bias to 5 and 7.1 kHz, collectively, most of the LC cells were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than those of the DC (Figure 5A, Mann-Whitney test: z=–11.34, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical comparison of frequency tuning between LC and DC with reference to a figure panel.

claim: The LC(microprism) showed cells of different response profiles to pure tones and AM-noise.
source: Using this integrated signal, we tested the ability of the cells of the LC (microprism) to respond to broadband noise at different AM rates within each cellular motif. Within the fraction of responsive cells, the LC(microprism) showed cells of different response profiles.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of cellular response diversity.

claim: Some cells in the LC(microprism) responded only to pure tones (tone-selective).
source: While some cells responded only to pure tones or tone-selective (Tone-sel), other cells responded only to AM-noise or noise-selective (Noise-sel).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of cellular response selectivity.

claim: Some cells in the LC(microprism) responded only to AM-noise (noise-selective).
source: While some cells responded only to pure tones or tone-selective (Tone-sel), other cells responded only to AM-noise or noise-selective (Noise-sel).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of cellular response selectivity.

claim: Some cells in the LC(microprism) responded to both pure tones and AM-noise (non-selective).
source: However, some cells responded to both pure tones and AM-noise (Non-sel), when the two stimuli were individually presented.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of cellular response selectivity.

claim: The LC(microprism) had similar fractions of noise-selective and non-selective cells, both significantly higher than tone-selective cells.
source: While the LC(microprism) had similar fractions of Noise-sel and Non-sel cells, both fractions were significantly higher than that of the Tone-sel cells (Figure 5B, one-way ANOVA, p=1.6 × 10–4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of cell type fractions with reference to a figure panel.

claim: Modules and matrix differentially process spectral information.
source: We also observed that modules and matrix differentially process the spectral information.
evidence: The manuscript states a general finding about functional differences between modules and matrix.

claim: The matrix had a significantly greater fraction of noise-selective cells compared to the modules.
source: For instance, the matrix had a significantly greater fraction of Noise-sel cells compared to the modules (Figure 5C, Mann-Whitney test, z=–2.32, p=0.02).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical comparison between modules and matrix with reference to a figure panel.

claim: Both modules and matrix had similar fractions of tone-selective and non-selective cells.
source: In contrast, both cellular motifs had similar fractions of Tone-sel and Non-sel cells (Figure 5C, Mann-Whitney test: z=0.48, p=0.62 for Tone-sel and z=1.36, p=0.17 for Non-sel).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons between modules and matrix with reference to a figure panel.

claim: Neurons in the matrix are more responsive to sounds of greater spectral and temporal complexity than those in the modules.
source: These findings suggest that neurons in the matrix are more responsive to sounds of greater spectral and temporal complexity than those in the modules.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental results about functional differences between matrix and modules.

claim: The DC showed significantly higher fractions of noise-selective and non-selective cells than tone-selective cells.
source: Similar to the LC, the DC showed significantly higher fractions of Noise-sel and Non-sel cells than Tone-sel cells, but the cellular fraction of Non-sel cells was higher than that of Noise-sel cells (Figure 5D, one-way ANOVA, f(2,9) = 86.9, p=1.2 × 10–6).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of cell type fractions in the DC with reference to a figure panel.

claim: The cellular fraction of non-selective cells in the DC was higher than that of noise-selective cells.
source: Similar to the LC, the DC showed significantly higher fractions of Noise-sel and Non-sel cells than Tone-sel cells, but the cellular fraction of Non-sel cells was higher than that of Noise-sel cells (Figure 5D, one-way ANOVA, f(2,9) = 86.9, p=1.2 × 10–6).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of cell type fractions in the DC with reference to a figure panel.

claim: Animals showed a lower fraction of responsive neurons to acoustic stimulation in the LC(microprism) compared to the DC regardless of sound type.
source: By pooling the cells based on their response to either pure tones or AM-noise, animals showed a lower fraction of responsive neurons to the acoustic stimulation in the LC (microprism) compared to the DC regardless of the sound type (two-way ANOVA, f(1,1,18) = 9.1, 7.8, and 0.1, p=0.007, 0.01, and 0.75 for region [LC vs DC], stimulus [pure tones vs AM-noise], and interaction, respectively, n=7 animals for LC and 4 animals for DC, the % of responsive cells ± SEM = 48±7% for LC and 75 ± 2% for DC).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing responsiveness between LC and DC.

claim: There were no significant differences between the number of tone or noise-responsive neurons between the LC(microprism) and LC(dorsal surface).
source: We observed that there were no significant differences between the number of tone or noise-responsive neurons between the LC(microprism) and LC(dorsal surface) (two-way ANOVA, f(1,1, 18)=0.07, 14.1, and 2.11, p=0.79, 0.001, and 0.16 for the region, stimulus [pure tones vs AM-noise], and interaction, respectively, n=7 animals for LC(microprism) and 4 animals for LC(dorsal surface), the % of responsive cells ± SEM = 48 ± 7% for LC(microprism) and 45 ± 11% for LC(dorsal surface)).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing responsiveness between different LC imaging approaches.

claim: The matrix has a greater proportion of spectrally modulated cells than modules.
source: For the LC(microprism), the matrix has a greater proportion of spectrally modulated cells (cells responding only to pure tones and unmodulated noise) than modules.
evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of spectral modulation between matrix and modules.

claim: The higher fractions of spectrally modulated cells in matrix were most prominent at sound levels below 70 dB.
source: The higher fractions of modulated cells in matrix were most prominently at sound levels below 70 dB (Figure 5E, two-way ANOVA: p=7.1 × 10–7, 1.0, and 0.01 for the region, sound level, and interaction, respectively), suggesting that the cells in the matrix have a lower threshold to detect the spectral features of sound.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to a figure panel and draws an inference about detection thresholds.

claim: Cells in the matrix have a lower threshold to detect the spectral features of sound.
source: The higher fractions of modulated cells in matrix were most prominently at sound levels below 70 dB (Figure 5E, two-way ANOVA: p=7.1 × 10–7, 1.0, and 0.01 for the region, sound level, and interaction, respectively), suggesting that the cells in the matrix have a lower threshold to detect the spectral features of sound.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental results about detection thresholds in matrix cells.

claim: The matrix had more cells responsive to temporal modulation as a main effect.
source: Similarly, the matrix had more cells responsive to temporal modulation (cells responding to AM-noise) as a main effect (Figure 5F, two-way ANOVA, p=2.7 × 10–4, 1.0, and 0.32 for the region, sound level, and interaction, respectively), which was consistent with the above results (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to figure panels.

claim: The DC and LC imaged via microprism were found to have different profiles of modulation of responses to spectral and temporal complexity.
source: The DC and LC imaged via microprism were found to have different profiles of modulation of responses to spectral and temporal complexity.
evidence: The manuscript states a general finding about functional differences between DC and LC.

claim: There is a general trend for SMI and TMI to decrease with increasing sound pressure level.
source: Although there is a general trend for SMI and TMI to decrease with increasing sound pressure level, corresponding to a decrease in the response to pure-tone and AM-noise, respectively, overall there is a statistically significant higher level of average SMI and TMI in the LC compared to the DC (Figure 5G and H, SMI: two-way ANOVA, p<0.001 for all region, sound level, and interaction, TMI: two-way ANOVA, p<0.001 for all regions, sound level, and interactions).
evidence: The manuscript reports a general trend and statistical analysis with reference to figure panels.

claim: There is a statistically significant higher level of average SMI and TMI in the LC compared to the DC.
source: Although there is a general trend for SMI and TMI to decrease with increasing sound pressure level, corresponding to a decrease in the response to pure-tone and AM-noise, respectively, overall there is a statistically significant higher level of average SMI and TMI in the LC compared to the DC (Figure 5G and H, SMI: two-way ANOVA, p<0.001 for all region, sound level, and interaction, TMI: two-way ANOVA, p<0.001 for all regions, sound level, and interactions).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing SMI and TMI between LC and DC with reference to figure panels.

claim: Neurons in the LC are more sensitive to spectral and temporal modulation than those in the DC.
source: These results suggested that neurons in the LC are more sensitive to spectral and temporal modulation than those in the DC.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental results about functional differences between LC and DC.

claim: Somatosensory inputs from many cortical and subcortical structures have been identified in the non-lemniscal division of the IC, particularly in the LC.
source: Somatosensory inputs from many cortical and subcortical structures have been identified in the non-lemniscal division of the IC, particularly in the LC (Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016; Lohse et al., 2022; Zhou and Shore, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that identified somatosensory inputs to the LC.

claim: Somatosensory projections mostly target the modules while auditory projections tend to target the matrix.
source: Previous work has shown that while somatosensory projections mostly target the modules, the auditory projections tend to target the matrix (Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016), which indicates that the LC is a multisensory integration site.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work showing differential targeting of projections to modules and matrix.

claim: The LC is a multisensory integration site.
source: Previous work has shown that while somatosensory projections mostly target the modules, the auditory projections tend to target the matrix (Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016), which indicates that the LC is a multisensory integration site.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from previous anatomical findings about the function of the LC.

claim: Auditory and somatosensory responses were evoked in the neurons of both matrix and modules imaged via microprism.
source: Auditory and somatosensory responses were evoked in the neurons of both matrix and modules imaged via microprism (Figure 7A, B, and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations with reference to figure panels.

claim: Both modules and matrix showed a higher fraction of auditory-selective cells than somatosensory-selective and auditory/somatosensory-nonselective cells.
source: Both modules and matrix showed a higher fraction of Aud-sel cells than that of Som-sel and Aud/Som-nonsel cells (Figure 7H, chi-square test, χ2=33.1, p=3.5 × 10–6).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to a figure panel.

claim: More auditory-responsive cells were found in the matrix, while more somatosensory-responsive cells were clustered in the modules.
source: Pooling the cells based on their auditory vs somatosensory responses revealed that more auditory-responsive cells (Aud-sel+Aud/Som-nonsel) were found in the matrix, while more somatosensory-responsive cells (Som-sel+Aud/Som-nonsel) were clustered in the modules (Figure 7B, D, F, and I, chi-square test, χ2=26.0, p=9.3 × 10–5), which was consistent with the reported difference in inputs to modules compared to matrix (Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to figure panels and cites previous work showing consistent anatomical findings.

claim: The distribution of auditory and somatosensory responsive cells was consistent with the reported difference in inputs to modules compared to matrix.
source: Pooling the cells based on their auditory vs somatosensory responses revealed that more auditory-responsive cells (Aud-sel+Aud/Som-nonsel) were found in the matrix, while more somatosensory-responsive cells (Som-sel+Aud/Som-nonsel) were clustered in the modules (Figure 7B, D, F, and I, chi-square test, χ2=26.0, p=9.3 × 10–5), which was consistent with the reported difference in inputs to modules compared to matrix (Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript compares current results with previous anatomical findings, supported by citation.

claim: Most of the acoustically responsive cells in the matrix showed onset responses.
source: Additionally, while most of the acoustically responsive cells in the matrix showed onset responses, the cells showing acoustically driven offset responses were clustered in the modules (Figure 7C and J, chi-square test, χ2=120.5, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to figure panels.

claim: Cells showing acoustically driven offset responses were clustered in the modules.
source: Additionally, while most of the acoustically responsive cells in the matrix showed onset responses, the cells showing acoustically driven offset responses were clustered in the modules (Figure 7C and J, chi-square test, χ2=120.5, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to figure panels.

claim: A higher fraction of auditory/somatosensory-nonselective cells in the modules had offset, not onset, auditory response than those located in the matrix.
source: Moreover, a higher fraction of Aud/Som-nonsel cells in the modules had offset, not onset, auditory response than those located in the matrix (chi-square test, χ2=13.2, p=0.004, % of Aud/Som-nonsel cells = 57%, 15%, 8%, and 20%, for auditory offset cells in modules, auditory onset cells in modules, auditory offset cells in matrix, and auditory onset cells in the matrix, respectively), which suggests a multisensory integrative function by those cells as discussed later.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis and draws an inference about multisensory integration.

claim: Matrix had a higher fraction of cells with suppressed responses than modules, while modules had a higher fraction of cells with enhanced responses.
source: However, matrix had a higher fraction of cells with suppressed responses than modules, while modules had a higher fraction of cells with enhanced responses (Figure 7G and K, chi-square test, χ2=12.9, p=0.04).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to figure panels.

claim: The LC(dorsal surface) shared common response profiles with the LC(microprism).
source: Consistent with the above data, the LC(dorsal surface) (Figure 8A–D, dorsolateral white rectangle) shared common response profiles with the LC(microprism).
evidence: The manuscript compares results from different imaging approaches with reference to figure panels.

claim: Both LC(dorsal surface) and LC(microprism) had a higher percentage of somatosensory responsive cells than the DC.
source: For instance, both regions had a higher percentage of somatosensory responsive cells than the DC (Figure 8A–D, dorsal yellow and dorsomedial blue rectangles) as quantitatively shown (Figure 8H, one-way ANOVA, p=0.02), which suggests that the LC is the main region of the IC shell that processes somatosensory information, consistent with the anatomical reports (Aitkin et al., 1978; Jain and Shore, 2006; Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to figure panels and cites previous anatomical studies.

claim: The LC is the main region of the IC shell that processes somatosensory information.
source: For instance, both regions had a higher percentage of somatosensory responsive cells than the DC (Figure 8A–D, dorsal yellow and dorsomedial blue rectangles) as quantitatively shown (Figure 8H, one-way ANOVA, p=0.02), which suggests that the LC is the main region of the IC shell that processes somatosensory information, consistent with the anatomical reports (Aitkin et al., 1978; Jain and Shore, 2006; Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from experimental results that is consistent with previous anatomical studies, supported by citations.

claim: Similar to the LC(microprism), the matrix and modules imaged from the dorsal surface had more percentage of auditory-selective cells than somatosensory-selective and auditory/somatosensory-nonselective cells.
source: Similar to the LC(microprism), the matrix and modules imaged from the dorsal surface had more percentage of Aud-sel cells than Som-sel and Aud/Som-nonsel cells (Figure 8E and I, chi-square test, χ2=86.1, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing results from different imaging approaches with reference to figure panels.

claim: Collectively, the matrix had more auditory responsive cells than modules, while modules had more somatosensory responsive cells than matrix when imaged from the dorsal surface.
source: Collectively, the matrix had more auditory responsive cells than modules, while modules had more somatosensory responsive cells than matrix (Figure 8J, chi-square test, χ2=66.5, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis with reference to a figure panel.

claim: Matrix regions of the LC were more responsive to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli than modules.
source: Here, using a novel microprism approach to image the LC in anesthetized and awake mice, we observed that (1) DC displayed tonotopic organization which was not consistently present in the LC, (2) DC neurons were generally more sound-responsive than LC neurons but that neurons in both regions had preferential responses to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli, (3) matrix regions of the LC were more responsive to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli than modules and that modules were more responsive to somatosensory stimuli, and (4) bimodal stimulation led to suppressive responses that were more prominent in the matrix.
